blocks.text: Molecules that leave the open surface of a liquid mix with the air above it; in an open vessel they keep leaving. In a closed system the escaped molecules gather above the surface, collide with the walls of the container and with the surface of the liquid, and may be recaptured by the surface, a process called condensation. Evaporation and condensation continue until the rate of evaporation equals the rate of condensation.

blocks.title: Vapour pressure
blocks.text: The pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid in equilibrium with the liquid at a given temperature is called the vapour pressure.

The magnitude of the vapour pressure does not depend on the amount of liquid in the container or on the volume of the container, nor on the surface area of the liquid: a larger surface presents a larger target for returning molecules, so the rate of condensation rises along with the rate of evaporation. In an evacuated closed vessel the system passes from an initial state with empty space above the liquid, through an intermediate state, to the equilibrium state in which evaporation and condensation are equal (Figure 5.8).

blocks.alt: Three closed containers with liquid at the bottom. (a) At the start the space above is a vacuum and molecules only leave the liquid (red arrows up). (b) Later vapour has built up and some molecules return (green arrows down). (c) At equilibrium as many molecules return as leave: evaporation and condensation rates are equal.
blocks.caption: Reaching equilibrium when a liquid evaporates in an evacuated closed vessel (original diagram after Figure 5.8).

blocks.prompt: Which liquid of each pair has the higher vapour pressure: alcohol or glycerine; petrol or kerosene; mercury or water? And which is more viscous, glycerine or kerosene?
blocks.explanation: The liquid with the weaker intermolecular forces evaporates more readily and has the higher vapour pressure: alcohol over glycerine (one O-H group against three), petrol over kerosene (smaller molecules, weaker London forces), water over mercury (metallic bonding holds mercury atoms far more strongly). Glycerine, with its three hydrogen-bonding O-H groups, is far more viscous than kerosene.

items: In a closed vessel evaporation and condensation reach equal rates; the vapour's pressure then is the vapour pressure, which depends on the liquid and the temperature but not on the amount of liquid, the vessel's volume or the surface area.
